text: AI governance roles look like close relatives of data governance roles, applied one layer up, to models instead of datasets. This lesson names them and shows exactly who's accountable for what.

The model owner is the business-side person accountable for a model's behavior and outcomes in production, not necessarily who built it. The model builder, a data scientist or ML engineer, develops and trains the model, the technical steward role applied to model artifacts. The independent validator reviews a model before it's trusted with real decisions, checking for the four risk categories from last lesson, separate from the people who built it.

The AI governance council, often legal, compliance, risk, and senior business leaders, approves new use cases, sets policy, and reviews incidents, the same role an existing data governance council already plays. Legal and compliance understand what laws might apply to a specific use case and flag it before deployment, not after.

Independence matters specifically here because the people who built a model are working from the same blind spots that produced it. If their intuition about normal data was off, they may not notice the model picked up that same skew. A useful rule of thumb: the model owner is accountable for the business outcome, the builder for technical quality, the council for whether the use case should have been approved at all.
Confusing these three, or leaving any unassigned, is one of the most common gaps found when a program is audited. Next up: how this connects to the data governance program you may already have.
